title: s-Block Elements
tagline: Alkali and alkaline earth metals: diagonal relationships, reactivity down the group and their compounds.

overview.intro: The s-block is the chemistry of electropositive elements: metals that lose their valence electrons easily and exist almost entirely as +1 and +2 ions. Because the valence configuration changes little down a group, the chemistry is remarkably uniform, and the interest lies in the trends — reactivity, solubility, thermal stability and the diagonal relationship that makes lithium resemble magnesium and beryllium resemble aluminium. This chapter works through group 1 and group 2 behaviour and then the compounds that the syllabus names, with the reason for each property traced back to size and charge density.

facts.label: Group 1
facts.value: Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr: one valence electron, +1 ions, stored under oil.

facts.label: Group 2
facts.value: Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba, Ra: two valence electrons, +2 ions, harder and higher melting.

facts.label: Diagonal relationship
facts.value: Li ~ Mg, Be ~ Al, B ~ Si, from similar charge-to-size ratios.

facts.label: Exam weight
facts.value: Compound chemistry of sodium and calcium plus trend explanations carry the marks.

learningOutcomes: Describe the physical and chemical trends in group 1 and group 2 with reasons based on size and ionisation energy.
Explain the diagonal relationship and give evidence for lithium–magnesium and beryllium–aluminium resemblance.
Account for the preparation and properties of sodium hydroxide, sodium carbonate and sodium bicarbonate.
Describe the preparation of calcium oxide, calcium hydroxide, calcium carbonate and calcium sulphate.
Explain the anomalous behaviour of beryllium and the inert-pair effect in the heavier members.

blocks.text: Both groups show the consequences of adding a whole electron shell at each step: size increases, ionisation energy falls, and the elements become more electropositive and more reactive. For group 1 this means the metal gives up its single valence electron with ever less energy, so lithium fizzes gently with water while caesium explodes, and the melting point falls down the group because the metallic bond weakens as the ion grows. Group 2 behaves the same way but with two electrons to lose: the metals are harder, the melting points higher than group 1 and more irregular, and the compounds more soluble in general because the +2 ion has higher lattice energy. Two anomalies matter. Beryllium forms covalent compounds rather than ionic ones because Be2+ is very small and highly polarising, and in the heavier p-block members the inert-pair effect makes the lower oxidation state more stable — a topic that reappears with thallium.

items: Ionisation energy falls down both groups, so reactivity increases down both.
Hydroxides become more basic down both groups: LiOH is weakly basic, CsOH strongly so.
Solubility of group 2 sulphates falls down the group while hydroxides become more soluble — the opposite directions are a favourite exam pairing.
Flame colours: Li crimson, Na golden yellow, K lilac, Rb red-violet, Ca brick red, Sr crimson, Ba apple green.
Group 2 metals are harder than group 1 because their +2 ions pack more charge into the lattice.
Carbonates and nitrates become more thermally stable down both groups because the larger cation polarises the anion less.

items.note: The reaction is vigorous and exothermic; the hydrogen may ignite because of the heat released.
Beryllium reacts only slowly because of a protective oxide film, and the product is covalent.

blocks.caption: Group 1 against group 2
rows: Soft, can be cut with a knife
Decompose on heating to the oxide

learn.title: The diagonal relationship and anomalous beryllium

blocks.text: A diagonal relationship exists because the two competing factors that determine chemical behaviour — size and charge — change in opposite directions along a diagonal. Moving right across a period, the ion shrinks and the charge rises, which increases polarising power; moving down a group, the ion grows and the charge stays the same, which decreases it. A period-2 element therefore resembles the period-3 element below and to the right of it: lithium resembles magnesium, beryllium resembles aluminium and boron resembles silicon. The evidence is chemical rather than superficial: lithium and magnesium both form nitrides directly with nitrogen, their carbonates and nitrates decompose on heating rather than melting, and their chlorides are more covalent and soluble in organic solvents than the rest of their groups. Beryllium mirrors aluminium in forming amphoteric oxides and in giving beryllates on reaction with alkali.

items: Li burns in nitrogen to give Li3N; Mg does likewise, no other alkali metal does.
Li2CO3 and BeCO3 decompose on heating, unlike the carbonates of the heavier group members.
BeO and Al2O3 are both amphoteric, dissolving in acids and in excess alkali.
BeCl2 and AlCl3 are covalent, covalent-dimeric and act as Lewis acids.
Beryllium forms the beryllate ion BeO2^2− in alkali, exactly as aluminium forms aluminate AlO2−.

items.text: Beryllium dissolves in sodium hydroxide solution
items.note: BeO + 2NaOH + 3H2O → Na2[Be(OH)4], releasing hydrogen, paralleling aluminium’s behaviour.
Li2CO3 → Li2O + CO2, unlike sodium carbonate which simply melts.

items.meaning: Similarity of a period 2 element with the element below-right of it.
Ability of a cation to distort the electron cloud of a neighbouring anion.
Reluctance of the ns^2 pair to take part in bonding in heavier p-block elements.
Oxide reacting with both acids and bases, such as BeO and Al2O3.

learn.title: Compounds of sodium: hydroxide, carbonate and bicarbonate

blocks.text: Sodium hydroxide is manufactured by the chlor-alkali process, in which brine is electrolysed; the castner-kellner cell uses a mercury cathode so that the sodium formed dissolves and can be run off to react with water, while the diaphragm cell keeps the chlorine and hydroxide apart. Sodium hydroxide is a strong base, highly soluble and deliquescent, attacking glass slowly to form sodium silicate, which is why stoppers must be plastic. Sodium carbonate, washing soda, is produced by the Solvay process, which passes ammonia and carbon dioxide into brine; sodium bicarbonate precipitates because it is the least soluble sodium salt in the mixture and then decomposes to the carbonate on heating. The whole cycle recovers ammonia by heating the ammonium chloride residue with lime, which is why the only raw materials consumed are salt and limestone. Sodium bicarbonate, baking soda, decomposes on heating or with acid to release carbon dioxide, which is the raising action in baking.

items: Chlor-alkali electrolysis: 2NaCl + 2H2O → 2NaOH + Cl2 + H2.
NaOH is deliquescent, strongly corrosive and stored in airtight containers.
Solvay raw materials: brine, ammonia and limestone; only NaCl and CaCO3 are consumed overall.
Solvay relies on sodium hydrogencarbonate being the least soluble sodium salt present.
NaHCO3 + HCl → NaCl + H2O + CO2, which is the basis of baking powder and of the antacid.
Anhydrous sodium carbonate is fused with silicon dioxide in the glass-making reaction.

items.note: 2NaHCO3 → Na2CO3 + H2O + CO2, the step that converts bicarbonate to washing soda.
Na2CO3 precipitates calcium as CaCO3, removing the permanent hardness.

learn.title: Compounds of calcium and the borax bead test

blocks.text: Calcium oxide, quicklime, is obtained by strongly heating limestone, an exothermic decomposition that reverses when lime is burned in air. Slaking it with water gives calcium hydroxide, slaked lime, whose solution is limewater — the standard test for carbon dioxide, turning milky as calcium carbonate precipitates and clearing again as excess carbon dioxide converts the solid to soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate. Calcium carbonate appears as limestone, marble and chalk, is insoluble in water and decomposes back to the oxide above about 840 °C, which is the reaction that drives lime kilns. Calcium sulphate exists as the hemihydrate plaster of Paris, which sets by reabsorbing water to become the dihydrate, and as gypsum, used to reduce the acidity of soil. The borax bead test closes the group: borax melts to a transparent glass of sodium metaborate, which dissolves transition-metal oxides to give characteristic coloured beads.

items: CaCO3 → CaO + CO2 above 840 °C; the reverse reaction is the lime cycle.
CaO + H2O → Ca(OH)2, strongly exothermic; the heat of slaking is used in self-heating tins.
Limewater turns milky with CO2 and clears with excess CO2 as calcium hydrogencarbonate forms.
Plaster of Paris, 2CaSO4·½H2O, sets to gypsum by taking up water.
Borax melts to sodium metaborate glass, which dissolves metal oxides to give a coloured bead.
Flame colours distinguish the members: calcium brick red, strontium crimson, barium apple green.

items.note: Ca(OH)2 + CO2 → CaCO3 + H2O gives the milkiness; excess CO2 gives Ca(HCO3)2 and the clear solution returns.
2CaSO4·½H2O + 3H2O → 2CaSO4·2H2O, crystallising into a hard mass for moulds and casts.

items.meaning: Calcium oxide, CaO, obtained by heating limestone.
Calcium hydroxide, formed by adding water to quicklime.
Aqueous calcium hydroxide, used to test for carbon dioxide.
Calcium sulphate hemihydrate, which sets by forming gypsum.

keyPoints: s-Block elements lose their valence electrons readily, giving +1 ions in group 1 and +2 in group 2.
Reactivity increases down both groups as ionisation energy falls.
Group 1 metals are soft with low melting points; group 2 are harder with higher melting points.
Flame colours identify members of both groups and arise from electron excitation and relaxation.
The diagonal relationship links Li–Mg and Be–Al through similar charge density.
Beryllium is anomalous: covalent compounds, amphoteric oxide and no reaction with water.
Sodium hydroxide comes from brine electrolysis; sodium carbonate from the Solvay process.
Limewater tests for carbon dioxide and clears in excess as hydrogencarbonate forms.
Plaster of Paris sets by absorbing water to become gypsum.
Carbonate and nitrate thermal stability increases down both groups as polarising power falls.
examFocus: Trend answers need size, then ionisation energy, then the observed property — in that order.
The diagonal relationship earns marks only when you cite evidence, not when you merely name it.
Solvay questions often ask why the process works: answer with the low solubility of sodium hydrogencarbonate.
For the limewater test, give both the milkiness and the clearing step with equations.

Decreasing tendency of the outer s electrons to bond in heavier p-block elements.
Reacting with both acids and bases, as beryllium oxide does.
Addition of water to quicklime to give slaked lime.
Glass of sodium metaborate used to detect transition-metal ions by colour.
Electrolysis of brine giving chlorine, hydrogen and sodium hydroxide.

questions.prompt: The general electronic configuration of the alkali metals is:
questions.explanation: Group 1 elements have a single electron in their outermost s orbital.

questions.prompt: Which pair of elements shows a diagonal relationship?
questions.explanation: Lithium and magnesium have similar charge-to-size ratios and share chemical behaviour not seen in the rest of their groups.

questions.prompt: Sodium carbonate is manufactured industrially by:
questions.explanation: The Solvay process uses brine, ammonia and limestone to precipitate sodium hydrogencarbonate, which is then calcined.

questions.prompt: Beryllium differs from the rest of group 2 because it:
options: Forms ionic compounds with a +2 ion
Forms covalent compounds and its oxide is amphoteric
Forms a stable carbonate that resists heating
questions.answer: Forms covalent compounds and its oxide is amphoteric
questions.explanation: The very small, doubly charged Be2+ has high polarising power, drawing the bonding electron pair towards itself and giving covalent character.

questions.prompt: The clear aqueous solution of calcium hydroxide used as the test for carbon dioxide is called __________ water.
questions.explanation: Limewater turns milky as calcium carbonate precipitates and clears with excess carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Quicklime is converted into slaked lime by adding water in a reaction called __________ .
questions.explanation: CaO + H2O gives Ca(OH)2 and releases a large amount of heat.

questions.prompt: Explain why the reactivity of group 1 metals increases down the group.
questions.answer: Each element down the group adds an electron shell, so the single valence electron lies further from the nucleus and is shielded by more inner shells. The first ionisation energy therefore falls, and the metal can shed its electron more easily, making the reaction with water or halogens progressively more vigorous.
questions.explanation: Size and shielding decide ionisation energy, and ease of electron loss decides reactivity.

questions.prompt: State two ways in which lithium resembles magnesium rather than sodium.
questions.answer: Lithium, like magnesium, combines directly with nitrogen to form a nitride, and its carbonate and nitrate decompose on heating instead of melting. Both also form chlorides with appreciable covalent character that dissolve in organic solvents.
questions.explanation: These are diagonal-relationship consequences of their similar charge density.

questions.prompt: Describe the Solvay process and explain why sodium hydrogencarbonate precipitates in it.
questions.answer: Ammonia is dissolved in brine to make it strongly alkaline, then carbon dioxide from burnt limestone is passed in. Ammonia, water, carbon dioxide and sodium chloride react to give sodium hydrogencarbonate and ammonium chloride. Sodium hydrogencarbonate is the least soluble of the sodium salts present under these conditions, so it crystallises out and is filtered off. On heating it converts to sodium carbonate, water and carbon dioxide. The filtrate is treated with slaked lime to recover ammonia, which returns to the saturator, so only sodium chloride and limestone are consumed overall.
questions.explanation: Solubility is the reason the process works, and ammonia recovery is the reason it is economical.

questions.prompt: Predict the products and explain the observations when excess carbon dioxide is passed through limewater, and write the equation for clearing.
questions.answer: Excess carbon dioxide first precipitates calcium carbonate as a white milkiness, since calcium carbonate is insoluble. Continued passage of carbon dioxide dissolves the precipitate because carbon dioxide reacts with water to form carbonic acid, which converts the insoluble carbonate into soluble calcium hydrogencarbonate, and the solution becomes clear again: CaCO3 + CO2 + H2O → Ca(HCO3)2. The same reaction explains the hardness of limestone regions and the formation of stalactites.
questions.explanation: Two competing reactions: precipitation first because carbonate is insoluble, then dissolution as hydrogencarbonate forms.
